name: São Tomé and Príncipe
summary: Two volcanic islands in the Gulf of Guinea, uninhabited until the Portuguese settled them around 1493; sugar and later cocoa plantations worked by enslaved and forced labour. Independent in 1975.

knownFor.label: Cocoa
knownFor.note: Once the world’s top cocoa producer (1908).

knownFor.label: Tchiloli
knownFor.note: Street theatre from a medieval play.

location.value: Gulf of Guinea on the equator; about 1,000 km².

terrain.value: Two volcanic islands with steep forested mountains; Pico de São Tomé rises to about 2,000 m, and the Obô rainforest covers the south.

climate.value: Hot and humid equatorial climate, with a long rainy season and a cooler dry season (the gravana) from about June to September.

resources.value: Fertile volcanic soil for cocoa, coffee, coconut and palm oil; rich fishing waters; possible offshore oil shared in a zone with Nigeria.

disasters.value: Few major disasters: heavy rains bring floods and landslides, and coastal erosion and rising seas threaten low shores.

population.value: About 230,000 people (2024 estimate), most of them on the larger island of São Tomé; Príncipe has only a few thousand.

urbanisation.value: Most people live in and around the capital.

disease.value: Good basic health care; rising diabetes.

migration.value: Many people move to Portugal and Angola for work and study; in colonial times thousands of contract workers came from Cape Verde, Angola and Mozambique.

economicBase.value: Cocoa is the main export, alongside coffee, fishing, small-scale farming and growing tourism; foreign aid is very important.

tradeRoutes.value: Ships through the port of São Tomé and flights to Lisbon, Luanda and Libreville; almost all fuel and much food are imported.

wealth.value: A small, aid-dependent lower-middle-income country; incomes rose after independence but remain modest.

moneyAndTax.value: The dobra, first issued in 1977; it has been pegged to the euro since 2010 and was redenominated as the “new dobra” in 2018.

inequality.value: Many people are poor, especially in former plantation communities, while incomes are higher in the capital.

governmentType.value: A semi-presidential republic: an elected president, a prime minister drawn from the National Assembly, and an autonomous Príncipe.

keyRulers.value: The first president led a one-party state under the MLSTP from independence (1975) until multi-party elections in 1991.

succession.value: Presidents and parliaments are chosen in multi-party elections, held regularly since the 1990 constitution and the 1991 vote.

institutions.value: The National Assembly, the presidency and government, a Constitutional Court, and Príncipe’s regional government (since 1995).

stability.value: A one-party state until 1990; since the first multi-party elections in 1991 power has changed hands peacefully at elections, despite coup attempts.

armyAndTech.value: Very small armed forces of a few hundred soldiers and a coast guard, helped by partners such as Portugal to patrol its waters.

majorWars.value: No wars since independence; the main violence came in colonial times, such as the Batepá massacre (1953), and in brief coup attempts.

territoryChange.value: No changes since independence; it agreed a joint oil development zone with Nigeria in 2001 instead of fixing a sea border there.

alliancesRivals.value: Close ties with Portugal and Angola; a member of the Community of Portuguese Language Countries; switched recognition from Taiwan to China (2016).

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state; it is better known for cocoa growing and its rich rainforest wildlife.

scienceEducation.value: Free primary schooling with high enrolment; higher education at the University of São Tomé and Príncipe, and many study in Portugal.

openness.value: Open to trade, aid and tourism; it depends heavily on imported food and fuel and on links with Portuguese-speaking countries.

communicationTransport.value: Coastal roads around São Tomé, an international airport in the capital, and short flights and boats to Príncipe.

religion.value: Mostly Roman Catholic since Portuguese times, with growing evangelical and other Protestant churches.

languageWriting.value: Portuguese is the official language; local creoles include Forro (Santome), Angolar and Principense, spoken alongside it.

artsArchitecture.value: Colonial plantation estates (roças) such as Roça Sundy and Agostinho Neto, and tchiloli street theatre based on a Charlemagne tale.

socialStructure.value: Descendants of enslaved and contract workers.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared island and Portuguese-speaking identity, with distinct groups such as the Forros, Angolares and descendants of contract workers.

dailyLife.value: Meals of fish, plantains, breadfruit and taro, often in stews such as calulu; many live by farming and fishing.

neighbours.value: Gabon is the nearest mainland; Equatorial Guinea’s islands of Bioko and Annobón lie close by, with Nigeria and Cameroon further north.

ideasReligions.value: Catholic Christianity brought by the Portuguese, mixed with African traditions; independence ideas came from African nationalist movements.

colonisation.value: Portuguese sailors reached the empty islands about 1470 and settlement began in 1493; sugar and later cocoa plantations used enslaved and contract labour until 1975.

riseSignals.value: After Portugal’s 1974 revolution the MLSTP negotiated independence, declared on 12 July 1975.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; cocoa exports were at their height in colonial times, around 1900–1910.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic, one of Africa’s smallest countries by area and population.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
